title: Science and Discovery
description: Ten reports, profiles, an interview and an essay about science and discovery: penicillin, a bird count, a young ant researcher, vaccine trials, a child's dinosaur bone, a kitchen experiment, scurvy, space exploration, a health scam and Dolly the sheep.

lessons.title: The Mold That Changed Medicine
lessons.summary: How a spot of mold on a forgotten dish in 1928 led, years later, to penicillin.
lessons.text:
Before 1940, even a small cut could be fatal. An infected wound could lead to an illness that no doctor was able to stop, and in times of war, many soldiers died not from their wounds but from the infections that followed. What changed this was a discovery that began, of all places, on a crowded laboratory bench in London.

In September 1928, a scientist from Scotland named Alexander Fleming returned from a summer vacation and began to sort through a pile of glass dishes on his bench. On these dishes, he had been growing bacteria, the tiny living things that cause many infections. One dish caught his eye. A spot of mold had grown on it, and around the mold there was a clear ring where the bacteria had died.

Nobody had planned this result. The mold had most likely drifted in through the air, so the discovery was purely a matter of chance. For Fleming, however, it was a revelation. Something in the mold was killing bacteria, and if it could kill them on a dish, perhaps it could kill them inside the human body as well. He named the substance penicillin, after the name of the mold.

The revelation did not lead to a cure at once. For about ten years, penicillin remained poorly understood and very hard to produce, and Fleming turned to other work.

Not until 1939 did serious work on penicillin commence again. At the University of Oxford, a team led by Howard Florey and Ernst Chain found a way to make it pure and stable. In 1941, they gave it to their first patient, a police officer who was severely ill after a small wound on his face had become infected. He began to recover, but the supply ran out, and he died. The drug worked, but far more of it was needed.

Large-scale production commenced in the United States, where companies learned to grow the mold in huge tanks. By June 1944, there was enough penicillin to treat the casualties of the Allied landings in France, and many severely wounded soldiers who in earlier wars might have died of infection went home alive. In 1945, Fleming, Florey and Chain shared the Nobel Prize.

Today, labs still use a version of Fleming's clear ring. To find out which drug will work against a patient's bacteria, a lab worker spreads the bacteria on a dish and places small paper disks on top, each disk containing a different drug. The next day, a clear ring has formed around some of the disks. The worker measures the diameter of each ring, because, in general, a larger diameter means that the bacteria are more sensitive to that drug. A disk with no ring at all shows a drug that will not help.

Had Fleming cleaned his dishes before his vacation, he might never have seen his ring, and medicine today might look very different.

Questions:
Why could a small cut be fatal before 1940?
It could lead to an infection that no doctor was able to stop.
Why was the discovery purely a matter of chance?
Nobody had planned it, and the mold had most likely drifted in through the air.
Why did little happen with penicillin for about ten years?
Penicillin was poorly understood and very hard to produce.
Who were the casualties that penicillin helped in 1944?
They were the soldiers wounded in the Allied landings in France.
How do labs use paper disks today?
They place disks containing different drugs on a dish of bacteria and measure the diameter of the clear ring around each disk.

lessons.title: One Day, Every Bird
lessons.summary: A retired teacher spends her 34th Christmas Bird Count counting birds by bicycle and by ferry.
lessons.text:
Every year, on a single day between the middle of December and the first days of January, tens of thousands of volunteers across North and South America go outside and count birds. The tradition is called the Christmas Bird Count. It began in 1900, when a bird expert named Frank Chapman suggested that people should count birds on Christmas Day instead of hunting them. Today, scientists use more than a century of these counts to see how bird populations are changing.

One of the most faithful counters in our area is Ruth Hale, a retired science teacher who has taken part for 34 years without missing a single count. Her friends gave her a nickname long ago: they call her "the Clock," because she is always ready before dawn. Ruth admits that the nickname is fair. On count day, she opens her curtains at 5 in the morning, makes coffee in her small cottage by the lake and waits for the first light.

Each count takes place inside a circle 15 miles in diameter, which is divided into sections. Ruth's section includes the pond behind her cottage, a stretch of forest and a small island in the lake. She reaches most of it on her bicycle. The island she reaches by ferry, which leaves the dock at 8 and returns at noon.

The pond is her favorite habitat to watch. Along its edge grow tall reeds, and in winter, small birds hide among the reeds to stay out of the wind. Ruth stands still for a long time, listening, because many birds are heard before they are seen. When something moves in the reeds, she notes its color, its size and the pattern of its feathers. A flash of bright red feathers, for example, usually means a cardinal.

The hardest part of the day is the island. From the ferry dock, a steep path climbs to the top of a rocky hill, where a different habitat, open grass and old pine trees, attracts different birds. Ruth is 71, and the path is steep, so she climbs it slowly and stops to rest. Once, in a light snow, she found a single gray feather on the path, and she has kept it inside a book ever since.

Why does she do it? "Because the birds cannot tell us what is happening to their habitat," she says. "We have to count them and find out." The numbers matter. Counts like hers have helped scientists show that many species are spending the winter farther north than they used to, as winters become warmer.

At noon, Ruth takes the ferry back, rides her bicycle home and adds up her totals: this year, 41 species and 1,263 birds. That evening, she draws the curtains, sits down by the fire and, as faithful as ever, marks next year's count on her calendar.

Questions:
When did the Christmas Bird Count begin, and why?
It began in 1900, when a bird expert suggested that people should count birds on Christmas Day instead of hunting them.
What is Ruth's nickname, and why do her friends use it?
Her nickname is "the Clock," because she is always ready before dawn.
How does Ruth reach the different parts of her section?
She reaches most of it on her bicycle, and she reaches the island by ferry.
Why do small birds hide among the reeds in winter?
They hide there to stay out of the wind.
What have counts like Ruth's helped scientists show?
They have helped show that many species are spending the winter farther north than they used to.

lessons.title: Ants, Paint and a Thesis: An Interview
lessons.summary: A young researcher talks about leaving a bank job to study how ants repair their trails.
lessons.text:
Amara Osei is 29 and in the final year of a research degree in biology at a large state university. She studies how ants find their way to food and back home again. We spoke in her workplace, a crowded lab full of plastic boxes, each holding a small ant colony.

How did you end up studying ants?

Quite late, compared with most scientists. After college, I worked for three years at a bank. It was a good job, but I was not genuinely happy there. One evening, I watched a line of ants crawl across my kitchen counter, and I realized that I cared more about where they were going than about anything I did at work. A month later, I decided to resign.

That must have been a hard decision.

It was. When I told my mother that I wanted to resign and study insects, there was a long silence on the phone, and then, to my surprise, laughter.

What does your research involve?

Ants leave chemical trails that other ants follow to food. I want to know what happens when a trail is broken. To follow individual ants, I mark each one with a tiny dot of paint, using a marker with an extremely fine tip. Then I film them as they crawl across a white board, and a computer program tracks every colored dot.

Does the marker hurt them?

No. We cool the ants first, so that they move slowly, and the paint is light and safe. Within a few minutes, they crawl back to work as if nothing had happened.

What is your thesis about?

My thesis asks a simple question: how do ants repair a broken trail? It sounds small, but the answer could help engineers design groups of robots that solve problems together, without a leader.

What is it like to work with your supervisor?

My supervisor, Professor Dana Klein, gives me a lot of freedom, but she also asks hard questions. When I showed her my first results, she asked whether I had genuinely tested my idea or only found what I wanted to see. That one question changed the direction of my thesis.

You came to the United States from Ghana. Has this country become home?

Yes. I came here for college at 18, and last year I received my citizenship, and the whole lab came to the ceremony. Afterward, there was cake and a lot of laughter, and someone had decorated the cake with small sugar ants.

What is your ambition now?

My ambition is to run my own lab one day, a workplace where students feel free to ask silly questions. But first, I have to finish the thesis.

Questions:
Why did Amara decide to resign from her job at the bank?
She was not genuinely happy there, and after watching ants crawl across her counter, she realized she cared more about them than about her work.
How does Amara follow individual ants?
She marks each ant with a tiny dot of paint, using a marker with a very fine tip, and films the ants as they crawl.
What question does her thesis ask?
Her thesis asks how ants repair a broken trail.
What happened after her citizenship ceremony?
There was cake and a lot of laughter, and the cake was decorated with small sugar ants.
What is Amara's ambition?
Her ambition is to run her own lab one day, a workplace where students feel free to ask silly questions.

lessons.title: How a Vaccine Is Tested
lessons.summary: A plain explanation of the stages a new vaccine passes through before, and after, it reaches the public.
lessons.text:
When a new vaccine appears in the news, people often ask the same question: how do we know it is safe? The short answer is that it has passed through a long series of tests, each larger than the one before.

The work begins in the laboratory. Scientists design a vaccine that teaches the body to recognize a particular virus or type of bacteria. Some vaccines contain a weakened or killed form of it; others contain only a small piece. Some use a harmless virus as a vector, a carrier that brings instructions into the body's cells to prepare them for the real threat. Whatever the design, the vaccine is tested on cells and animals first.

Only then do tests on people begin. In the first phase, a small group of healthy adult volunteers, usually 20 to 100, receives the vaccine. The main goal is safety: researchers want to clarify which dose is safe and which side effects, such as a sore arm, appear. In the second phase, several hundred people take part, and the researchers clarify the best dose and schedule. In the third phase, thousands of volunteers are divided at random into two groups. One group receives the vaccine; the other receives a placebo, a shot with no active ingredient. Usually, neither the volunteers nor their doctors know who received which, so that their expectations cannot affect the results.

The size of each trial is calculated in advance, so that the trial is large enough to show a real difference between the two groups. No trial has unlimited time or unlimited money.

During the trial, an independent board of experts reviews the results as they arrive. These advisers do not work for the company that makes the vaccine, and they have the power to terminate a trial early. They may terminate it if serious safety problems appear, or if the vaccine works so clearly that it would be unfair to keep giving the placebo. Any modification to the trial's plan must also be explained and approved.

When the trial ends, the company sends its data to government experts, who in the United States also ask a committee of outside advisers for their opinion. A company cannot simply assert that its vaccine works; it has to show the evidence.

Even after approval, the testing does not stop. Doctors keep reporting health problems that appear after a shot, so that rare side effects can be found. Some vaccines, like the flu vaccine, need a small modification every year to match the viruses that are spreading.

What makes doctors confident is consensus: many studies, by different teams in different countries, reaching the same conclusion. When experts assert that a vaccine is safe, it is that consensus they are relying on.

Questions:
What is a vector in a vaccine?
It is a harmless virus that carries instructions into the body's cells.
What do researchers want to clarify in the first phase?
They want to clarify which dose is safe and which side effects appear.
Why is the size of a trial calculated in advance?
It is calculated so that the trial is large enough to show a real difference between the two groups.
When can the advisers terminate a trial early?
They can terminate it if serious safety problems appear, or if the vaccine works so clearly that giving the placebo would be unfair.
What makes doctors confident about a vaccine?
Consensus makes them confident: many studies by different teams reaching the same conclusion.

lessons.title: Nora and the Bone in the Creek
lessons.summary: On a family vacation, a nine-year-old finds a dinosaur bone and helps scientists bring it out safely.
lessons.text:
Nora Burke was nine when she found the dinosaur. She and her parents were spending a week at a small inn in eastern Montana, a region known for its fossils, and on the third morning she went for a walk along a dry creek behind the inn with her father.

About half a mile along, Nora noticed something dark brown sticking out of the side of the creek, a little above her head. It was not an ordinary stone; it looked like a fragment of something much bigger.

Her father wanted to pull the fragment out, but Nora stopped him. Her class had visited a museum that spring, and a guide had explained that a fossil taken out of the ground loses much of its value to science, because scientists learn a great deal from exactly where and how it lies. So they took photos, measured how far the fragment was from the path, and walked back to the inn.

The owner of the inn knew the family who owned the land and called them at once. They gave their permission, and that afternoon Nora's father sent the photos to a natural history museum two hours away. The next morning, a fossil expert named Sam Reyes arrived with two students, a ladder and a box of tools.

Because the bone was high up, the team set the ladder against the rock, and Reyes climbed up to look. After a few minutes, he called down that the fragment was part of a limb bone, probably from the back leg of a young duck-billed dinosaur that had lived more than 65 million years ago. The piece that showed was only about as thick as Nora's wrist, but the rest of the limb was still inside the rock.

It is slow work to retrieve a bone that old, because the fossil can break as easily as dry clay. Over two days, the team cleared the rock around it with small brushes, wrapped the bone in strips of cloth and wet plaster, and let the plaster dry into a hard shell. Only then could they safely retrieve it.

Afterward, Reyes answered Nora's questions. Was her dinosaur an ancestor of birds? Not quite, he explained. Birds came from a different group of dinosaurs, small hunters that ate meat, so the ancestors of today's birds were only distant cousins of Nora's plant-eating dinosaur.

Before the family left, the museum gave Nora a certificate for her good deed. Leaving the bone in place, Reyes told her, was the most important part of that deed. At home, Nora put the certificate above her bed, next to a photo of herself on the ladder, holding her wrist next to the bone to show its size.

Questions:
Where was Nora staying when she found the bone?
She was staying with her parents at a small inn in eastern Montana.
Why did Nora stop her father from pulling the fragment out?
A museum guide had explained that a fossil taken out of the ground loses much of its value to science.
What was the fragment part of?
It was part of a limb bone, probably from the back leg of a young duck-billed dinosaur.
How did the team retrieve the bone safely?
They cleared the rock with small brushes, wrapped the bone in cloth and wet plaster and let the plaster dry into a hard shell.
Why did the museum give Nora a certificate?
It gave her a certificate for her good deed of leaving the bone in place.

lessons.title: Three Jars on a Kitchen Shelf
lessons.summary: A father and his daughter use bread dough to learn how a fair experiment works.
lessons.text:
Last month, my daughter Lily, who is ten, came home with a task from school. Her class had just finished a module on the scientific method, and the final part of the module was an experiment to be done at home. The rules were simple: ask a question, make a prediction, test it fairly and report the results.

Lily found her question while watching me bake bread. "Why do you always use warm water?" she asked. I told her that warm water helps the yeast work faster. Yeast is a tiny living thing that feeds on sugar and produces gas, and the gas is what makes dough rise. "How do you know?" she asked. To be honest, I did not. It was simply what my mother had always done.

So that became the question: does the temperature of the water change how fast dough rises? Lily's prediction was that the warmest water would work best.

We used three identical glass jars. Into each jar went the same amount of flour, sugar and yeast. Lily measured the water in a plastic measuring cylinder, filling the cylinder to the same line each time. The only difference was the temperature: cold water for the first jar, warm water for the second and very hot water for the third. Changing only one thing, her teacher had explained, is what makes a test fair.

The placement of the jars mattered too. If one jar stood next to the warm oven and another by a cold window, we would not know whether the water or the placement had caused the difference. So we put all three jars side by side on the same shelf, far from the oven. Lily drew a line on each jar with a marker to show where the dough began, and she propped her notebook against the bread box so that she could write while she watched.

Then we set a kitchen timer for 15 minutes. Lily sat in front of the jars, listening to the timer tick. Each time it rang, she marked the new height of the dough on each jar. The timer seemed to tick louder with every minute.

After one hour, the results were clear. The dough in the warm jar had doubled. The dough in the cold jar had barely risen. What Lily had not expected was the hot jar, in which the dough had not risen at all. Her prediction had been only partly right: heat helps yeast, but water that is too hot kills it.

That evening, Lily typed up her results and printed a chart on our old printer. As always, the printer took several minutes. Then she propped the chart against the jars for a photo.

The next morning, we made bread in the oven and ate it as toast. Lily announced that the toast tasted better because science had proven it. I did not argue.

Questions:
What had Lily's class just finished at school?
They had just finished a module on the scientific method.
What was the only difference between the three jars?
The only difference was the temperature of the water.
Why did the placement of the jars matter?
If one jar stood next to the warm oven, they would not know whether the water or the placement had caused the difference.
What did Lily not expect?
She did not expect that the dough in the hot jar would not rise at all.
Why was Lily's prediction only partly right?
Heat helps yeast, but water that is too hot kills it.

lessons.title: A Fair Test at Sea
lessons.summary: How a navy doctor in 1747 ran one of the first fair tests in medicine, and why it took decades to matter.
lessons.text:
Around 1750, a long trip at sea was a brutal experience. The men of a ship's crew lived for months in crowded, wet spaces below deck, close to the ship's hull, where the air was bad and there was little light. Their food was mostly salted meat and hard dry bread, often full of insects. For many of them, the worst danger was not storms or enemy ships but a disease called scurvy.

Scurvy began slowly. A man felt tired and weak. Then his mouth began to hurt and bleed, dark marks appeared on his skin, and his legs and ankles swelled and became so painful that he could hardly stand. A long bout of the disease left men too miserable and weak to work, and many died.

In 1747, a navy doctor from Scotland named James Lind decided to test some of the cures that people suggested. On board the ship Salisbury, he chose 12 men who had scurvy and whose cases were as similar as possible. All of them were suffering a severe bout of the disease. They were kept in the same part of the ship, near the hull, and given the same basic food. Then he divided them into six pairs and gave each pair a different treatment: cider, vinegar, sea water, a mixture containing acid, a paste of spices, or two oranges and a lemon every day.

The results were remarkable. Within about a week, one of the two men who ate the fruit was fit for duty, and the other was well enough to help care for the rest. The others remained miserable.

What makes Lind's test famous today is not only its result but its design. By comparing similar patients who lived under the same conditions, he made sure that the treatment was the only important difference between them. It is often described as one of the first controlled trials in medicine.

Yet the obstacles to change were large. Fresh fruit was an expensive commodity, hard to store at sea, and Lind himself was not fully sure that fruit alone was the answer. A second obstacle was that nobody understood nutrition in the modern sense. The idea that the body needs small amounts of certain substances to sustain good health was still far in the future. As a result, it was not until 1795 that the Royal Navy began to give its men lemon juice every day. After that, scurvy became rare on its ships, and lemons became an important commodity for any long trip.

Today, we know that scurvy is caused by a lack of vitamin C, which the human body cannot make for itself. A diet with enough fruit and vegetables is enough to sustain healthy levels. Had the navy understood nutrition earlier, many brutal trips would have been far less deadly.

Questions:
Why was a long trip at sea brutal around 1750?
The crew lived for months in crowded, wet spaces near the hull, ate poor food and often suffered from scurvy.
What happened to a man's legs and ankles during scurvy?
They swelled and became so painful that he could hardly stand.
How did Lind make his test fair?
He chose similar patients, kept them in the same part of the ship and gave them the same basic food.
Which treatment worked best?
Two oranges and a lemon every day worked best.
What were two obstacles to change?
Fresh fruit was an expensive commodity, and nobody understood nutrition in the modern sense.

lessons.title: Is Space Worth the Money?
lessons.summary: An essay that weighs the case against spending on space exploration and the case for it.
lessons.text:
Every time a large rocket launch fills the news, an old question returns with it: should a country spend money on exploring space while people on Earth still go hungry? It is a fair question, and both sides deserve to be heard.

The case against is easy to understand. Hunger has not disappeared, even in rich countries, and many schools and hospitals need support. To some critics, it seems pathetic, or at least selfish, that a society can send machines to other planets while some of its families cannot afford dinner. Their argument is not that space is boring, but that money spent there is money not spent here. Others point out that space exploration has sometimes been driven less by curiosity than by ideology. The race to the Moon, for example, was largely a contest between two political systems, each eager to prove that its own ideology was better.

There is also a newer concern. Today, much of the activity in space is led not by governments but by private companies, several of them owned by titans of the technology industry. When a businessman spends billions on rockets, critics ask whether the goal is to benefit humanity or simply to make one businessman richer and more famous. A few titans, they argue, should not decide the future of space.

The case in favor begins with the numbers. In the United States, the national space agency receives less than half of one percent of the federal budget. Even if all of that money were moved elsewhere, it would not end hunger, which depends as much on politics, war and distribution as on monetary resources. The problem, in other words, is not purely monetary.

Supporters also argue that space research produces innovative technology that helps people on Earth. Weather satellites warn of storms and save lives, and other satellites help farmers watch their crops. Many innovative products, from better water filters to the tiny cameras in our phones, were developed or improved with the help of space programs.

Finally, there is a longer view. Some thinkers believe that a civilization limited to one planet is doomed sooner or later, whether by a large rock from space or by its own mistakes. Others reply that we are not doomed at all if we take care of the planet we have.

Where does this leave us? In my view, the choice is not between space and hunger. A wise civilization can do both, as long as it remains honest about why it is going to space and about who benefits. Not only does space research teach us about the universe, but it also forces us to ask what kind of society we want to be.

Questions:
Why do some critics call spending on space pathetic or selfish?
They think it is wrong to send machines to other planets while some families cannot afford dinner.
What role did ideology play in the race to the Moon?
The race was largely a contest between two political systems, each eager to prove that its ideology was better.
What do critics ask about a businessman who spends billions on rockets?
They ask whether the goal is to benefit humanity or simply to make him richer and more famous.
Why would moving the space budget not end hunger?
Hunger depends as much on politics, war and distribution as on monetary resources.
What do some thinkers believe about a civilization limited to one planet?
They believe it is doomed sooner or later.

lessons.title: The Powder That Promised Everything
lessons.summary: A columnist explains how her aunt fell for a health scam, and the warning signs they both learned.
lessons.text:
Last spring, my aunt Helen, who is 68 and very sharp, fell for a health scam. I am writing about it with her permission, because the methods of such scams are subtle, and smart people fall for them every day.

It began with a blogger. Helen had been reading a popular blog about healthy eating, and the blogger, a friendly woman with beautiful photos of her kitchen, seemed genuinely kind. Over several months, however, her posts changed. At first, they offered simple recipes. Then they began to suggest that dairy products were the hidden cause of tiredness, pain and even serious disease. Finally, an advertisement appeared at the top of every post for a natural powder that would remove the effects of dairy and, the advertisement claimed, reduce the need for prescription drugs.

Helen ordered a three-month supply for 180 dollars. Worse, she stopped taking her blood pressure pills, a prescription from her own doctor, because the blogger had written that the powder did the work that pills only pretended to do. Two weeks later, she felt weak at the grocery store, fell, and was taken to the hospital in an ambulance. Luckily, she was not badly hurt. The doctor at the hospital put her back on her prescription at once.

When Helen asked for a refund, the company pointed to a clause in its terms: a refund was available only for packages that had not been opened, returned within 7 days. She had opened the first package on the day it arrived. The clause was legal, but it was written in tiny gray letters at the very bottom of the company's website.

What makes a scam work is rarely one big lie. More often, it is a series of subtle steps: trust built slowly, an ordinary food turned into an enemy, and a product that seems to solve every problem at once. Some people genuinely cannot digest dairy well, and they are right to avoid it, but that is very different from the claim that milk is secretly harming everyone.

Since then, Helen and I have learned the warning signs. Be careful when a product promises to cure many different problems, when it claims that doctors are hiding the truth, or when it tells you to stop medicine that a doctor gave you.

Can anyone punish such companies? Sometimes. In the United States, a federal agency can punish companies that make false health claims in their advertisements. Helen reported the company, and a few months later she got most of her money back through her credit card company.

The most important lesson, however, has nothing to do with money. Before you stop taking any prescription, talk to your doctor. A powder can be sent back; a fall cannot.

Questions:
How did the scam begin?
It began with a blogger who seemed genuinely kind and who slowly started to blame dairy products for many problems.
What did the advertisement claim?
It claimed that the powder would remove the effects of dairy and reduce the need for prescription drugs.
Why was Helen taken to the hospital in an ambulance?
She had stopped taking her blood pressure pills, and she felt weak and fell at the grocery store.
Why did the company refuse Helen a refund?
It pointed to a clause saying that a refund was available only for packages that had not been opened, returned within 7 days.
Who can punish companies that make false health claims?
In the United States, a federal agency can punish them.

lessons.title: A Seemingly Ordinary Sheep
lessons.summary: The life of Dolly, the first mammal cloned from an adult cell, and what scientists learned from her.
lessons.text:
On July 5, 1996, a lamb was born at a research institute near Edinburgh, in Scotland. She was small, white and seemingly ordinary, and few people knew at first that she was anything more. Her name was Dolly, and she was the first mammal ever cloned from a cell taken from an adult animal.

To understand why Dolly mattered, it helps to know what cloning means. Every cell in a sheep's body carries the same genetic instructions, but most cells have become specialized: a skin cell does the work of skin, and a blood cell the work of blood. Many scientists doubted that this process could be reversed. Technically, sheep and some other mammals had been cloned before, but only from cells taken from very young embryos, which had not yet become specialized. Dolly was technically something new.

The team, led by Ian Wilmut and Keith Campbell, took a cell from the milk-producing tissue of a six-year-old sheep. They took an egg cell from a second sheep, removed its genetic material, and joined the two cells with a small electric pulse. The new cell began to divide and was placed inside a third sheep, who later gave birth to Dolly. It was far from easy: out of 277 attempts, only one produced a living lamb, and that lamb was Dolly.

The confirmation that Dolly was a true clone came in two forms. The first was visible to anyone: Dolly had a white face, like the sheep that had given the cell, while the mother who gave birth to her had a black face. The second confirmation came from genetic tests.

When the news was announced in February 1997, the reaction around the world was enormous. Many people disliked the idea of cloning, and some feared that the cloning of humans would follow. Wilmut himself said that he disliked the idea of cloning people, and that his goal was to produce animals that could make medicines in their milk.

For the most part, Dolly lived a seemingly normal life. She had six lambs of her own, born in the usual way. However, she later developed a lung disease, and in February 2003, at the age of six, she was put to sleep. Her death caused real grief among the staff who had cared for her every day, and many people around the world shared that grief.

Today, Dolly stands in a glass case at the National Museum of Scotland in Edinburgh. She has become a kind of monument, not to one person but to years of patient work by a whole team. Visitors often make the same small gesture when they reach her: they lean closer to the glass, as if she might move. It is a quiet gesture of curiosity, and perhaps the best monument a scientist could hope for.

Questions:
When and where was Dolly born?
She was born on July 5, 1996, at a research institute near Edinburgh, in Scotland.
Why was Dolly technically something new?
Sheep and some other mammals had been cloned before, but only from very young embryos, while Dolly was cloned from an adult cell.
What was the first confirmation that Dolly was a true clone?
Dolly had a white face, like the sheep that had given the cell, while her birth mother had a black face.
What did many people think of the news in 1997?
Many people disliked the idea of cloning, and some feared that the cloning of humans would follow.
What gesture do many visitors make when they reach Dolly?
They lean closer to the glass, as if she might move.
